title: Sudden Vision Loss: Treat It as an Emergency
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Sudden painless or painful vision loss is not a routine eye complaint. Protect the patient from injury, identify associated neurologic or ocular red flags, and escalate urgently for time-sensitive evaluation.
recognize: Curtain-like vision loss, flashes/floaters, monocular blackout, severe eye pain, headache, nausea, or focal neurologic deficits are high-risk patterns.
priorities: Treat abrupt vision change as urgent and compare onset, laterality, pain, and neurologic symptoms.
Prevent falls and driving.
assessMonitor: Assess visual change description, pupils, pain, neurologic status, trauma history, and vascular symptoms within scope.
interventions: Arrange urgent ophthalmic/emergency evaluation according to presentation.
medicationSafety: Do not instill non-prescribed eye drops that could delay diagnosis or worsen some conditions.
teaching: Any sudden vision loss warrants immediate evaluation even if it improves.
delegationScope: Acute vision-loss triage and escalation require licensed nursing judgment; facility/state policy governs eye-medication tasks.
examTrap: Scheduling routine follow-up for abrupt vision loss because the eye looks normal externally.
oneLinePearl: Sudden vision loss is an emergency until proven otherwise.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Ophthalmology acute-eye safety principles

title: Retinal Detachment Cues: Flashes, Floaters, Curtain
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: New flashes, a sudden increase in floaters, or a shadow/curtain across vision can signal retinal tear or detachment and requires urgent ophthalmic evaluation.
recognize: Symptoms are often painless and may begin peripherally.
Recent eye surgery, trauma, or high myopia can increase risk.
priorities: Escalate new curtain-like field loss or sudden flashes/floaters promptly.
Protect from falls and avoid delay for routine visual testing.
assessMonitor: Clarify onset, eye affected, field-loss pattern, trauma/surgery history, and progression.
medicationSafety: Eye drops do not treat retinal detachment and should not delay referral.
teaching: Flashes and floaters that are new or suddenly worse need prompt evaluation.
delegationScope: Recognition and escalation are licensed-nurse responsibilities.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient because there is no eye pain.
oneLinePearl: Retinal detachment can be painless and still be vision-threatening.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Ophthalmology retinal emergency guidance

title: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma: Pain Plus Vision Change
bottomLine: Severe eye pain, blurred vision/halos, headache, nausea/vomiting, and a red eye can indicate acute angle closure. Rapid pressure-lowering treatment and ophthalmic evaluation are required to prevent permanent optic-nerve damage.
recognize: The presentation is usually abrupt and markedly symptomatic compared with chronic open-angle glaucoma.
priorities: Escalate immediately for emergency eye evaluation.
Review medications that can precipitate angle closure in susceptible patients when relevant.
assessMonitor: Assess onset, pain, nausea, visual symptoms, pupil asymmetry, and medication history within scope.
interventions: Administer ordered pressure-lowering therapy and monitor response when authorized.
medicationSafety: Do not delay definitive evaluation while treating nausea or headache alone.
redFlags: Red eye with acute vision loss
teaching: This symptom cluster needs emergency care, not routine clinic follow-up.
delegationScope: Acute glaucoma treatment authority follows state/facility policy; PN/LVN role centers recognition, authorized treatment, and escalation.
examTrap: Treating nausea and headache without recognizing the eye emergency.
oneLinePearl: Painful red eye plus halos and nausea = pressure emergency.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Ophthalmology angle-closure guidance

title: Chemical Eye Exposure: Irrigate Immediately
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Chemical eye injury is a decontamination emergency. Begin copious irrigation immediately; identifying the chemical is useful, but irrigation should not be delayed when corrosive exposure is suspected.
recognize: Pain, tearing, redness, blurred vision, blepharospasm, or known chemical splash require urgent action.
priorities: Start irrigation immediately and remove contaminated contact lenses when feasible.
Continue emergency evaluation after decontamination.
assessMonitor: Monitor pain, vision changes, exposure type/time, and response during irrigation.
interventions: Use copious water or appropriate irrigation solution while lifting lids as needed per protocol.
medicationSafety: Do not attempt chemical neutralization with another chemical.
teaching: At home or work, start flushing immediately and seek urgent medical care.
delegationScope: Emergency irrigation may follow protocol; ongoing eye assessment and escalation require licensed care.
examTrap: Waiting to identify the exact chemical before irrigating.
oneLinePearl: Chemical in the eye? Water first, details second.

title: Orbital Trauma: Protect the Eye and Avoid Pressure
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Eye or orbital trauma with decreased vision, irregular pupil, penetrating object, severe pain, diplopia, or proptosis requires urgent evaluation. Suspected globe injury must be protected without applying pressure.
recognize: Visible penetrating object, teardrop pupil, new vision loss, marked swelling, or inability to move the eye normally are concerning.
priorities: Do not remove embedded objects or apply pressure to a suspected open globe.
Protect with a rigid shield if available and escalate urgently.
assessMonitor: Assess mechanism, vision change, pain, pupils, bleeding, and associated head injury within scope.
interventions: Keep the patient from rubbing the eye and support urgent specialty evaluation.
medicationSafety: Avoid ocular manipulation or drops unless ordered when open-globe injury is suspected.
teaching: Do not press, rub, or remove an embedded object.
delegationScope: Eye-trauma assessment/escalation requires licensed nursing judgment.
examTrap: Applying a pressure patch to a suspected globe rupture.
oneLinePearl: Suspected open globe: shield, don't press.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Ophthalmology ocular-trauma principles

title: Sudden Hearing Change: Separate Wax From Emergency
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Abrupt unilateral hearing loss, especially with tinnitus, vertigo, neurologic symptoms, or no obvious conductive cause, requires prompt evaluation rather than routine earwax treatment.
recognize: Cerumen and middle-ear fluid can cause conductive loss, but sudden sensorineural loss is time-sensitive.
priorities: Clarify onset, laterality, associated vertigo/tinnitus, trauma, medication exposure, and neurologic symptoms.
Escalate abrupt unexplained loss promptly.
assessMonitor: Assess communication ability, ear symptoms, neurologic cues, and medication history within scope.
interventions: Use communication aids while arranging evaluation.
medicationSafety: Review potentially ototoxic medications and exposures when hearing changes occur.
teaching: Sudden hearing loss should not wait for a routine appointment.
delegationScope: Recognition and escalation require licensed nursing judgment.
examTrap: Assuming all new hearing loss in older adults is chronic presbycusis.
oneLinePearl: Sudden hearing loss is not normal aging.

title: Ototoxic Exposure: Hearing and Balance Are Safety Signals
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Some medications and workplace chemicals can damage hearing or balance. New tinnitus, hearing change, or disequilibrium during exposure should trigger medication/exposure review and timely escalation.
recognize: Aminoglycosides, selected chemotherapy drugs, loop-diuretic exposure, solvents, and other ototoxicants can contribute depending on dose and context.
priorities: Report new auditory or vestibular symptoms and review concurrent noise/chemical exposure.
Use required PPE and hearing protection in occupational settings.
assessMonitor: Trend tinnitus, hearing, balance, renal function when drug-related, and exposure history.
interventions: Support ordered audiology monitoring and exposure reduction.
medicationSafety: Do not independently stop essential medications; escalate for prescriber review.
teaching: Report tinnitus or new balance problems early.
delegationScope: Medication/exposure interpretation requires licensed nursing judgment and prescriber/occupational-health collaboration.
examTrap: Waiting for profound deafness before reporting tinnitus.
oneLinePearl: Tinnitus can be an early toxicity cue.

title: Ear Infection Complications: Watch Beyond the Earache
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Most uncomplicated ear infections improve without major complication, but worsening pain, swelling behind the ear, new facial weakness, severe headache, neck stiffness, or persistent systemic illness requires reassessment for extension beyond the middle ear.
recognize: Hearing reduction can occur with middle-ear fluid; mastoid-area swelling or protruding pinna is more concerning.
priorities: Monitor symptom trajectory and red flags rather than pain score alone.
Escalate neurologic, mastoid, or systemic deterioration.
assessMonitor: Track fever, pain, drainage, hearing, mastoid tenderness/swelling, and neurologic symptoms.
interventions: Administer ordered analgesics/antibiotics and reinforce follow-up.
medicationSafety: Do not reuse leftover antibiotics or assume all ear pain needs antibiotics.
teaching: Seek reevaluation if symptoms worsen or new swelling/hearing problems develop.
delegationScope: Routine observations may be delegated; complication recognition/escalation requires licensed nursing judgment.
examTrap: Calling persistent worsening symptoms expected because ear infections are common.
oneLinePearl: Common infection does not mean complications are harmless.

title: After Cataract Surgery: Know the Warning Signs
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Mild irritation can occur after cataract surgery, but sudden vision loss, severe or increasing pain, marked redness, flashes/floaters, nausea, or purulent drainage requires prompt ophthalmic contact.
recognize: Postoperative warning signs can indicate infection, pressure rise, or retinal complication rather than normal recovery.
priorities: Reinforce eye-protection and medication instructions.
Escalate major pain or vision deterioration promptly.
assessMonitor: Monitor vision trend, pain, redness, drainage, medication adherence, and protective restrictions.
interventions: Administer ordered eye drops using clean technique and avoid contaminating the bottle tip.
medicationSafety: Verify drop sequence and spacing when multiple ophthalmic medications are prescribed.
teaching: Do not rub the eye; use the shield and activity restrictions exactly as instructed.
delegationScope: Ophthalmic medication administration follows state/facility policy; deterioration requires prompt escalation.
examTrap: Reassuring severe pain as normal postoperative discomfort.
oneLinePearl: After cataract surgery, severe pain or vision loss is never routine.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Ophthalmology postoperative cataract-care principles

title: Hearing Impairment: Communication Is a Patient-Safety Intervention
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: Hearing impairment can create medication, consent, fall, and discharge errors. Improve the communication environment, verify hearing devices, face the patient, and use teach-back rather than assuming nodding means understanding.
recognize: Misheard instructions may look like confusion, nonadherence, or cognitive impairment.
priorities: Reduce background noise, face the patient, speak clearly, verify hearing aids, and use written/visual supports when helpful.
Use qualified interpretation rather than family substitution when language access is also needed.
assessMonitor: Assess preferred communication method and understanding of high-risk instructions.
interventions: Use teach-back for medications, procedures, and discharge plans.
medicationSafety: Confirm names/doses in writing when hearing limits verbal medication teaching.
teaching: Bring hearing devices and communication preferences to healthcare visits.
delegationScope: Communication support can involve the whole team; evaluation of understanding remains the licensed nurse's responsibility.
examTrap: Speaking louder from behind the patient instead of improving communication conditions.
oneLinePearl: Communication access is clinical safety, not courtesy.
